methods.name: __init__
methods.signature: __init__(sample_size: int | tuple[int, int] = 32, in_channels: int = 1, out_channels: int = 1, act_fn: GenerativeActivation = 'relu', prior: FlowPrior = 'logistic', input_dim: int = 784, num_coupling_layers: int = 4, num_hidden_layers: int = 5, hidden_dim: int = 1000, input_reorder: Literal['tile', 'none'] = 'tile', init_range: float = 0.01)

members.extended:
Defaults reproduce the paper's MNIST experiment (Figure 3): 784
dimensions, four coupling layers whose coupling networks have five
hidden layers of 1000 rectified units, and a standard logistic prior.

Args:
    input_dim: Dimensionality `D` of the data the flow is defined
        on — the paper's "# dimensions" row and the released
        configs' `nvis`.  Figure 3: `784` (MNIST), `2304`
        (TFD), `3072` (SVHN, CIFAR-10).  Must be even, since every
        coupling layer splits it in half.
    num_coupling_layers: Number of stacked additive coupling layers.
        The paper uses `4` for every dataset; three is the minimum
        that lets all dimensions interact.
    num_hidden_layers: Hidden layers inside each coupling network
        `m`.  Paper Figure 3: `5` for MNIST, `4` for TFD /
        SVHN / CIFAR-10.
    hidden_dim: Units per hidden layer of `m`.  Paper Figure 3:
        `1000` (MNIST), `5000` (TFD), `2000` (SVHN,
        CIFAR-10).
    input_reorder: One-off permutation applied before the first
        coupling layer.  `"tile"` (default) reproduces the paper's
        odd/even partition; `"none"` splits in raster order, which
        is what the released configs for SVHN / CIFAR-10 do.
    init_range: Half-width of the uniform weight initialisation of
        every coupling network, matching the official release's
        `irange = 0.01`.  Biases start at zero, and the diagonal
        scaling starts at `s = 0` (identity).

Notes:
    NICE is defined on flat `D`-vectors, not on a pixel grid: both
    the paper and the released configs parametrise each experiment by
    a single dimension count.  `input_dim` is therefore the only
    dimensional knob, and the spatial fields inherited from
    `GenerativeModelConfig` (`sample_size`, `in_channels`,
    `out_channels`) hold the equivalent vector encoding rather than
    an image shape the sources never state: `sample_size` is pinned
    to `(1, input_dim)`, and channels other than 1 are refused.
examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice._config import NICEConfig
>>> cfg = NICEConfig()
>>> cfg.model_type
'nice'
>>> cfg.in_channels
1

members.name: NICEForImageGeneration

methods.name: generate
methods.signature: generate(n_samples: int = 1, device: str | None = None)
methods.summary: Sample `n_samples` vectors by inverting a prior draw.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: Number of samples to draw.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
Where to allocate the prior sample.  Defaults to the device the
model's parameters are on.

returns.description:
`samples` of shape `(n_samples, D)`, in the same
(dequantised, possibly whitened) space the model was trained
on — no squashing is applied.  Reshape to the dataset's image
grid for display.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import (
...     NICEConfig, NICEForImageGeneration,
... )
>>> cfg = NICEConfig(input_dim=64, num_coupling_layers=2,
...                  num_hidden_layers=1, hidden_dim=16)
>>> model = NICEForImageGeneration(cfg).eval()
>>> samples = model.generate(n_samples=3).samples
>>> samples.shape  # flat, like the training data
(3, 64)
>>> samples.reshape(3, 1, 8, 8).shape  # onto an 8x8 grid for display
(3, 1, 8, 8)
>>> _ = lucid.manual_seed(0)
>>> first = model.generate(n_samples=2).samples
>>> _ = lucid.manual_seed(0)  # the prior draw is the only randomness
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(first, model.generate(n_samples=2).samples))
True

members.summary: NICE with the exact maximum-likelihood loss and `.generate()`.
members.extended:
Wraps `NICEModel` with the paper's training objective — plain
negative log-likelihood, no bound and no auxiliary term — and the
ancestral sampler.  `forward(x)` returns a
`NormalizingFlowOutput` whose `loss` is
`-log_prob.mean()`; `generate(n_samples)` draws
$h \sim p_H$ and returns $f^{-1}(h)$ in a single parallel
pass.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Architecture and prior; see `NICEConfig`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import (
...     NICEConfig, NICEForImageGeneration,
... )
>>> cfg = NICEConfig(input_dim=64, num_coupling_layers=2,
...                  num_hidden_layers=1, hidden_dim=16)
>>> model = NICEForImageGeneration(cfg).eval()
>>> out = model(lucid.rand((2, 64)))
>>> out.loss.shape                       # scalar NLL
()
>>> model.generate(n_samples=3).samples.shape
(3, 64)
notes:
Reference: Dinh, Krueger, and Bengio, *"NICE: Non-linear Independent
Components Estimation"*, ICLR Workshop, 2015 ([arXiv:1410.8516](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8516)).

Training objective (maximised in the paper, minimised here):



$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B}
    \Big[\log p_H\big(f(x^{(b)})\big) + \sum_{i=1}^{D} s_i\Big].
$$

The paper optimises this with Adam (learning rate $10^{-3}$)
for 1500 epochs and reports test log-likelihoods of 1980.50 (MNIST),
5514.71 (TFD), 11496.55 (SVHN) and 5371.78 (CIFAR-10) nats — figures
that are only comparable under the paper's own preprocessing.

members.name: NICEModel

methods.name: input_dim
methods.summary: Flattened dimensionality `D` the bijection acts on.

methods.name: prior
methods.summary: Name of the factorised latent prior (`"logistic"` / `"gaussian"`).

methods.name: encode
methods.summary: Map data to the latent space.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Dequantised samples, shape `(B, D)`.

returns.description:
`(h, log_det)` with `h` of shape `(B, D)` and
`log_det` of shape `(B,)`.  Every coupling layer and
permutation contributes exactly zero to `log_det`, so it is
the diagonal scaling's $\sum_i s_i$ broadcast across the
batch.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import NICEConfig, NICEModel
>>> cfg = NICEConfig(input_dim=64, num_coupling_layers=2,
...                  num_hidden_layers=1, hidden_dim=16)
>>> model = NICEModel(cfg).eval()
>>> _ = nn.init.normal_(model.scaling.log_scale, std=0.1)  # s = 0 at init
>>> x = lucid.rand((2, 64))
>>> h, log_det = model.encode(x)
>>> h.shape, log_det.shape
((2, 64), (2,))
>>> bool((log_det == model.scaling.log_scale.sum()).all().item())
True
>>> bool(lucid.allclose(model.decode(h), x, atol=1e-5))  # exact inverse
True

methods.name: decode
methods.summary: Invert the flow — latent `(B, D)` back to data `(B, D)`.
methods.extended:
Exact rather than approximate: every stage is run backwards, so
`decode(encode(x)[0])` recovers `x` up to float round-off.

methods.name: log_prob
methods.summary: Exact per-sample log-likelihood $\log p_X(x)$ in nats.

members.summary: Bare NICE flow — invertible map plus the factorised latent prior.
members.extended:
The prior is part of the model rather than of the training loop
(matching the official `NICE(encoder, prior)` construction): the
flow only becomes a density once the latent space is measured against
$p_H$.  Three entry points cover the two directions and the
density:

* `encode(x) -> (h, log_det)` — data to latent, with the per-sample
  log-determinant of the transformation.
* `decode(h) -> x` — the *exact* inverse, back to `(B, D)`.
* `log_prob(x) -> (B,)` — exact log-likelihood in nats.

Data and latent are both flat `(B, D)` — the flow has no notion of
spatial structure, so image batches are flattened by the caller.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description:
Architecture and prior.  `config.input_dim` must be even; see
`NICEConfig` for the full field list.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import NICEConfig, NICEModel
>>> cfg = NICEConfig(input_dim=64, num_coupling_layers=2,
...                  num_hidden_layers=1, hidden_dim=16)
>>> model = NICEModel(cfg).eval()
>>> x = lucid.rand((2, 64))
>>> h, log_det = model.encode(x)
>>> h.shape, log_det.shape
((2, 64), (2,))
>>> model.log_prob(x).shape
(2,)
notes:
Reference: Dinh, Krueger, and Bengio, *"NICE: Non-linear Independent
Components Estimation"*, ICLR Workshop, 2015 ([arXiv:1410.8516](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8516)).

The exact objective, with additive couplings contributing zero:



$$
\log p_X(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{D}
    \Big[\log p_{H_i}\big(f_i(x)\big) + s_i\Big].
$$

The model expects *dequantised* data — the paper adds uniform noise of
`1/256` and rescales to $[0, 1]^D$ ($1/128$ and
$[-1, 1]^D$ for CIFAR-10), and applies ZCA (SVHN, CIFAR-10) or
approximate whitening (TFD) beforehand.  Feeding raw 8-bit integers
lets the flow put unbounded density on the quantisation lattice, so
the likelihood diverges.

attributes.name: couplings
attributes.description:
`config.num_coupling_layers` additive coupling layers, each
followed by an index reversal.

attributes.name: scaling
attributes.description:
Diagonal scaling $\exp(s)$ closing the stack — the only
stage contributing to the log-determinant.

members.name: nice_cifar
members.summary: Construct the NICE flow for the CIFAR-10 setup.
members.extended:
Paper-faithful CIFAR-10 configuration from Dinh et al., 2014
Figure 3: 3072 dimensions, four coupling layers with four hidden
layers of 2000 units each, and a standard logistic prior.

parameters.name: pretrained
parameters.description:
No checkpoint is published for `nice_cifar`, so `True` raises
`NotImplementedError` rather than return randomly initialised weights.

parameters.name: **overrides
parameters.description:
Optional `NICEConfig` field overrides forwarded into the
underlying config.

returns.description:
Bare bijection configured with the CIFAR-10 setup and any
overrides.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import nice_cifar
>>> model = nice_cifar(input_dim=64, hidden_dim=16).eval()
>>> x = lucid.rand((1, 64)) * 2.0 - 1.0
>>> model.log_prob(x).shape
(1,)
notes:
Reference: Dinh, Krueger, and Bengio, *"NICE: Non-linear Independent
Components Estimation"*, ICLR Workshop, 2015 ([arXiv:1410.8516](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8516)),
Figure 3.  Reported test log-likelihood: 5371.78 nats, on ZCA-whitened
data dequantised with uniform `1/128` noise and rescaled to
$[-1, 1]^D$ (CIFAR-10 is the one dataset given the wider
range).  The released reference config for this dataset instead
stacks 8 coupling layers of 2400 units with a normal prior and no
input reordering — see the module docstring for how far overrides
reproduce it.

members.name: nice_cifar_gen
members.summary: NICE generator for the CIFAR-10 setup (NLL loss + `.generate()`).
members.extended:
Same bijection as `nice_cifar`, wrapped with the exact
maximum-likelihood objective and the ancestral sampler.  This is the
weakest of the four experiments in perceptual terms — NICE's
volume-preserving couplings cannot model natural-image texture — and
the reason RealNVP replaced additive couplings with affine ones.

parameters.name: pretrained
parameters.description:
No checkpoint is published for `nice_cifar_gen`, so `True` raises
`NotImplementedError` rather than return randomly initialised weights.

parameters.name: **overrides
parameters.description:
Optional `NICEConfig` field overrides forwarded into the
underlying config.

returns.description: Generator configured with the CIFAR-10 setup and any overrides.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.nice import nice_cifar_gen
>>> model = nice_cifar_gen().eval()
>>> out = model.generate(n_samples=2)
>>> out.samples.shape
(2, 3072)
notes:
Reference: Dinh, Krueger, and Bengio, *"NICE: Non-linear Independent
Components Estimation"*, ICLR Workshop, 2015 ([arXiv:1410.8516](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.8516)),
Figure 3.  Reported test log-likelihood: 5371.78 nats on ZCA-whitened
data in $[-1, 1]^D$.

summary: NICE family — Dinh, Krueger & Bengio, 2014 (additive-coupling flow).
citation: Dinh, Laurent, David Krueger, and Yoshua Bengio. "NICE: Non-linear Independent Components Estimation." International Conference on Learning Representations, Workshop Track, 2015.
theory:
NICE is the first *normalizing flow* trained on images: instead of
bounding the likelihood (VAE) or factorising it over pixels
(autoregressive models), it learns an invertible map
$h = f(x)$ onto a latent space with a factorised prior, so the
exact data log-density falls straight out of the change-of-variables
formula



$$
\log p_X(x) = \log p_H\big(f(x)\big)
    + \log\Big|\det \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big|.
$$

Nothing is approximated — no variational gap, no Markov chain — but
every layer now has to be invertible *and* have a cheap Jacobian
determinant, which is a severe architectural constraint.

The construction that satisfies both is the **additive coupling
layer**.  Partition the dimensions into two blocks
$(x_{I_1}, x_{I_2})$ and update only the second, conditioned on
the first:



$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{I_1} &= x_{I_1}, \\
y_{I_2} &= x_{I_2} + m(x_{I_1}).
\end{aligned}
$$

The Jacobian is unit lower-triangular, so its determinant is
$1$ no matter how deep the coupling network $m$ is, and
the inverse is the same graph with one sign flipped,
$x_{I_2} = y_{I_2} - m(y_{I_1})$.  Since one block passes
through untouched, consecutive layers must exchange the roles of the
two blocks; at least three couplings are required before every
dimension can influence every other, and the paper stacks four with
deep rectified networks (linear output units) as the $m$'s.

A stack of volume-preserving maps is itself volume-preserving, so
NICE closes the flow with a learned **diagonal scaling**
$h = \exp(s) \odot h^{(4)}$ — the only stage that moves the
determinant:



$$
\log p_X(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{D}
    \Big[\log p_{H_i}\big(f_i(x)\big) + s_i\Big].
$$

The scales $\exp(s_i)$ behave as learned per-dimension
importance weights: directions the model captures well are given
small scale, making $s$ the non-linear analogue of an
eigenvalue spectrum in PCA.  The prior is a standard logistic
(heavier tails, used for MNIST / SVHN / CIFAR-10) or a standard
normal (used for TFD).

Generation is exact and parallel — draw $h \sim p_H$, return
$f^{-1}(h)$ — with no decoder and no iterative refinement.  The
coupling layer introduced here is the direct ancestor of RealNVP
(affine couplings, multi-scale spatial masks) and Glow (invertible
1x1 convolutions); the samples look blurry by modern standards, but
the recipe defined how exact-likelihood generative models are built.
